title: AI Risk Management Guide: How to Choose the Right AI & Machine Learning Platform
description: Practical ai risk management guidance: decision criteria, implementation steps, risks, evaluation checks, and a usable go/no-go checklist. Updated October 2026.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Create an inventory of AI use
sections.body: List AI systems used by employees, embedded in purchased software, or connected to internal data. For each, record the business owner, purpose, users, data types, provider, model or feature, external integrations, and whether output affects customers or consequential decisions. Include unofficial tools and features enabled inside existing subscriptions. An inventory makes risk review concrete and prevents the team from applying one generic control to very different use cases.

sections.title: Classify risk by impact
sections.body: Assess what could happen if the system is wrong, manipulated, unavailable, or exposes data. A drafting assistant for internal brainstorming has a different risk profile from a system that ranks job applicants, approves credit, handles medical information, or can execute production actions. Rate impact, likelihood, exposure, and detectability separately; record the reasoning and the person who accepted any residual risk. Escalate high-impact use cases for legal, security, privacy, and domain review before deployment.

sections.title: Protect data and access
sections.body: Map the data sent to the model, retrieved by connectors, stored in logs, and returned to users. Minimize the data collected, restrict access by role, remove secrets from prompts, and verify provider retention, training, deletion, and subprocessors in current contract terms. Test whether one user can retrieve another user's documents through search or retrieval. Keep credentials out of model context and require explicit authorization before AI-generated actions can read, change, or transmit sensitive resources.

sections.title: Test misuse and failure cases
sections.body: Create tests for prompt injection, malicious documents, data leakage, fabricated citations, biased or inconsistent output, unsafe tool calls, and unexpected inputs. Test the entire application—including retrieval, permissions, logging, and downstream actions—not just the model in isolation. Record the expected safe behavior for each test and retest after model or prompt changes. A red-team exercise is useful only when findings have owners, severity, remediation dates, and evidence that the fix works.

sections.title: Keep humans accountable
sections.body: Define when a person must review output, how that person sees supporting evidence, and how to reject or correct a recommendation. Avoid rubber-stamp approval by giving reviewers enough time, context, and authority to disagree. For decisions that materially affect people, provide a clear escalation or appeal path and retain the records needed to investigate an error. Responsibility remains with the organization deploying the system; a vendor's general assurance is not a substitute for local controls.

sections.title: Monitor and respond to incidents
sections.body: Track quality failures, refusal behavior, data access anomalies, latency, cost spikes, user reports, and changes in usage. Decide in advance who can disable the feature, revoke credentials, switch providers, and notify affected parties. Keep logs proportionate to the risk and avoid retaining sensitive prompts indefinitely without a justified purpose. Exercise the incident plan with a realistic scenario so that a safe shutdown does not depend on one engineer being available.

sections.title: Document evidence and ownership
sections.body: Maintain a risk register that links each identified risk to a control, control owner, evidence, test date, and residual-risk decision. Verify applicable laws and sector rules with qualified counsel rather than relying on a generic checklist. Require vendors to explain relevant data processing, security measures, service boundaries, and change notifications. Reassess when the use case, model, data sources, permissions, user population, or legal environment changes.

sections.title: Go-live gate
sections.body: Do not launch until the system has an approved owner and purpose, data handling is reviewed, high-severity tests are addressed, access and logging are configured, reviewers know their responsibilities, and a rollback or disable path is proven. Set review dates and conditions that trigger reassessment. A practical AI risk program is a continuous cycle of inventory, evaluation, mitigation, monitoring, and learning—not a one-time policy document or a claim that a tool is 'safe' in every context.
